assessment.nobel_worthiness: Changed how economists and policymakers understand the labour-market effects of trade exposure and technology. It combined credible research designs with large, replicated effects on employment, wages and local communities, and it influenced policy and political debate well beyond economics.
assessment.attribution: The China-shock work is closely tied to Autor, Dorn and Hanson. Autor also anchors the task-based and technology strand. Katz and others have important parallel contributions on wage inequality, so the credit boundary is contestable.
assessment.maturity: Roughly fifteen years of citations, replications and refinements. The core findings are well tested, though some magnitudes and their persistence have been debated.
uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers a prize centred on the task-based framework, which would shift credit toward other scholars.
Ongoing debate over the size and interpretation of the trade-shock effects.
The three-person limit excludes Katz and other major contributors.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework with nominal rigidities underpins modern monetary policy analysis and central-bank practice. It combines a pricing model, a policy-rule perspective and a micro-founded synthesis.
assessment.attribution: Credit is spread across many people: Calvo (staggered pricing), Taylor (the policy rule and staggered contracts), Woodford (the synthesis and optimal-policy analysis), Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets (empirical and estimated DSGE models). Any three-person selection is a judgement call and leaves out major contributors.
assessment.maturity: Very mature, with decades of practical use in policy institutions and heavy citation. Several related prizes (Lucas, Kydland-Prescott, Phelps, Sargent-Sims) already cover adjacent ground.
uncertainties: Difficulty of allocating credit among more than eight plausible names.
The framework's reputation after the post-2008 and post-2021 inflation experiences.
Overlap with earlier macroeconomics prizes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Foundational intertemporal open-economy macroeconomics. It established the standard analytical framework for current accounts, exchange rates and international policy transmission, and it identified the exchange-rate disconnect puzzles that still organise the field.
assessment.attribution: The pair is clean and well matched. The Foundations of International Macroeconomics textbook, the 'New Open Economy Macroeconomics' and the disconnect puzzles are jointly and individually associated with both. Rogoff also appears in the separate crisis-history candidacy.
assessment.maturity: Thirty years of influence. The framework is part of standard graduate training and policy modelling.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees the contribution as a field-defining framework or as a synthesis of existing ideas.
Rogoff's work on crises overlaps with another ballot and may split support.
Fewer clean identification-based results than other candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Created modern formal political economics: how electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity shape fiscal policy and economic outcomes. The work links theory to comparative empirical evidence. It is high-impact beyond economics, notably in political science and comparative institutions research.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the central pair through their joint books and papers. Besley is a close complement on state capacity and political incentives. The trio is coherent, although Acemoglu and Robinson, already honoured in 2024, shaped the adjacent territory.
assessment.maturity: Very mature, with more than three decades of work and a large empirical follow-on literature, including natural-experiment evidence.
uncertainties: Partial overlap with the 2024 prize on institutions may reduce marginal appeal.
Whether the empirical constitutional-effects results are seen as robustly causal.
My own field proximity should not be taken as merit evidence; it is judged here on the same criteria as other fields.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity transformed trade theory and empirics by explaining selection, exporter productivity premia and a new channel for gains from trade. The framework is widely used in quantitative trade and policy analysis.
assessment.attribution: Melitz's 2003 model is the central contribution. Helpman has long-standing related contributions on trade with firm-level heterogeneity, and Redding is a significant extender. Helpman also appears under B049, which complicates the attribution picture.
assessment.maturity: More than twenty years of citations and empirical validation, and well integrated into the field.
uncertainties: Krugman's 2008 prize on new trade theory may be seen as overlapping.
Possible competing credit for Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, who are not listed here.
Helpman's candidacy is split across ballots.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Built long-run top-income series from tax records and reoriented the study of inequality in economics and public debate. The work is empirically important and highly influential for policy discussion, though more descriptive than causal.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez are the original top-incomes pair. Zucman's contributions on wealth and offshore holdings are important but more recent and could be added or substituted. Many others contributed to the data effort, notably Atkinson, who is deceased.
assessment.maturity: The top-income series are two decades old and widely replicated. The wealth-tax and offshore-wealth parts are newer and still disputed.
uncertainties: Methodological debate about the measurement and interpretation of top shares and wealth.
Whether the contribution is judged more descriptive than explanatory.
Saez also appears on other ballots, which dilutes attribution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Formalised present bias and reference-dependent preferences and linked them to saving, consumption and policy design. The work extended the behavioural economics honoured in 2002 and 2017 and informed practical interventions such as default retirement saving.
assessment.attribution: Laibson (quasi-hyperbolic discounting) and Rabin (psychology-informed models and, with Koszegi, reference dependence) are the most central. Koszegi, O'Donoghue and Loewenstein have significant and contested claims.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with long citation histories and many field and lab replications. Some welfare and policy interpretations remain contested.
uncertainties: Prior behavioural prizes (Kahneman, Thaler) may reduce the appetite for another in this area.
Difficult attribution among five or more credible names.
Replication and external-validity debates in parts of behavioural economics.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Combined machine learning with causal inference through double/debiased ML, heterogeneous-effect estimation and causal forests. These methods are now widely used across applied fields, and the work builds on the 2021 prize for causal inference.
assessment.attribution: Chernozhukov (with co-authors on double ML) and Athey (with Wager, causal forests and policy learning) are the main architects. Many co-authors (for example Imbens, Newey and Hansen) are not named, and Wager is a younger collaborator.
assessment.maturity: Relatively recent, about a decade of influence. Adoption is rapid, but long-term durability is less certain than for older candidates.
uncertainties: Possibly premature relative to older candidates.
Overlap with the 2021 causal-inference prize.
Attribution among many co-authors, and Athey's presence on another ballot.
